html:
Antwerp at the centre is the chart's name for the decades, roughly 1500 to 1569, when the port of Antwerp in the Low Countries (now Belgium) was the main marketplace of Europe. In Fernand Braudel's history, it took over from Venice as the heart of the European economy.

Antwerp rose because others brought their goods to it. The king of Portugal made it the outlet for the pepper and spices his ships brought round Africa from India. German merchants, above all the Fugger family of Augsburg, brought silver and copper from central Europe, which the Portuguese needed to buy spices in Asia. English cloth came over to be finished and sold. Antwerp owned few ships of its own; the trade came to it.

What it left:

  • A permanent exchange, the Bourse, opened in a new building in 1531, where merchants met daily.
  • A large money market, where kings, including Charles V, borrowed.
  • A boom in printing, painting and luxury trades.

Its fortunes swung with the spice trade and with the finances of Spain, whose kings ruled the Low Countries. The Spanish crown's bankruptcy of 1557 shook it. Then came religious unrest and the Dutch revolt; the end date marks the slide into war. Spanish troops sacked the city in 1576, and after the Spanish took it back in 1585 the Dutch closed the river Scheldt. Merchants and money moved north, and the centre passed to Amsterdam.
